Claws
klôz
n. pl. (the divided hoof of a clean beast; the talons of a bird; the nails of a man under judgment)
Old English clawu. The KJV uses the word for the cloven hoof of Deuteronomy 14, for birds' talons, and for the nails Nebuchadnezzar grew in his madness — the mark, in every case, of what a creature is.

Biblical Definition

The law used claws to mark the clean: “every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat” (Deu 14:6) — the same rule Leviticus states as “whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is clovenfooted, and cheweth the cud” (Lev 11:3). Daniel uses them to mark a man unmade: Nebuchadnezzar “was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen… till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws” (Dan 4:33). Zechariah uses them to mark a shepherd who devours his own flock: “he shall eat the flesh of the fat, and tear their claws in pieces” (Zec 11:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a claw as the sharp hooked nail of a beast or bird, and in another sense the whole foot of an animal armed with hooked nails.

expand to see more

CLAW, n. The sharp hooked nail of a quadruped, bird or other animal.

CLAW, n. The whole foot of an animal armed with hooked nails.

CLOVENFOOTED, a. Having the foot divided into two parts, as an ox.

Key Scripture

Deu 14:6 — "And every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat."

Dan 4:33 — "The same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: and he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws."

Zec 11:16 — "For, lo, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, which shall not visit those that be cut off, neither shall seek the young one, nor heal that that is broken, nor feed that that standeth still: but he shall eat the flesh of the fat, and tear their claws in pieces."

Dan 7:19 — "Then I would know the truth of the fourth beast, which was diverse from all the others, exceeding dreadful, whose teeth were of iron, and his nails of brass; which devoured, brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with his feet;"

Modern Corruption

The king who said, is not this great Babylon that I have built, was given the nails of a bird and put out to grass until he knew who reigns.

expand to see more

Daniel 4 is the fullest treatment in Scripture of what pride does to a man and what God does to pride. Nebuchadnezzar walks in his palace, says is not this great Babylon that I have built by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty, and the word is still in his mouth when the sentence falls. He is driven from men, his hair grows like feathers, his nails like birds' claws, and he eats grass as oxen until he knows that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men. The restoration is as remarkable as the judgment: he lifts up his eyes to heaven, his understanding returns, and he blesses the King of heaven, all whose works are truth and His ways judgment.

The corruption to name is the doctrine that man is the measure and the maker of his own greatness. It is not a modern invention — Babel said it first, and Babylon said it best — but it is unusually well housed in a culture that speaks of building one's own truth and authoring one's own identity. Daniel 4 answers with an image rather than an argument: a man who will not acknowledge that he is a creature is given the outward form of a beast until he does. And the chapter is written in the first person, by the king, after the fact.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew parsah (H6541), hoof; Aramaic tephar (H2953), nail, claw; Hebrew garam (H1633), to break the bones, tear in pieces.

expand to see more

Hebrew parsah (H6541) — hoof, cloven claw; Deuteronomy 14:6, Leviticus 11:3.

Aramaic tephar (H2953) — nail, claw; Daniel 4:33, 7:19.

Hebrew garam (H1633) — to break bones, tear in pieces; Zechariah 11:16, Numbers 24:8.

Hebrew gerah (H1625) — the cud; Leviticus 11:3, Deuteronomy 14:6.

Aramaic shelet (H7981) — to rule, have dominion; Daniel 4:17, 4:25.

Usage

"“Cleaveth the cleft into two claws” — the law's mark of a clean beast."

"“His nails like birds' claws” — a king reduced until he confessed heaven rules."

"“Tear their claws in pieces” — Zechariah's worthless shepherd."
